title: What should you ask first in a cost or operations case, and which trap should you avoid?
description: The first question to ask in a cost and operations case, how to structure it, and the trap to avoid.
hook: Ask first what the goal is: lower cost, more capacity, or better reliability, because each points you at a different part of the operation. The trap is cutting costs that carry revenue, or speeding up a step that was never the bottleneck.
body:
The first question to ask

Is the goal lower cost, more output, or more reliable service, and by how much?

Cost and operations cases are about doing the same work for less, or doing it better. "Cut costs by 10%" sends you to the biggest cost lines. "Ship more orders" sends you to the bottleneck. "Stop late deliveries" sends you to variability and failure points. A target and a deadline also tell you whether quick fixes are enough or the client needs a structural change.

How to build your structure

  1. Map the cost base or the process: what are the biggest cost lines, or the steps from start to finish?
  2. Benchmark each line or step against peers, past performance or capacity.
  3. Start with the biggest gap.
  4. List levers: people, process, technology, suppliers.
  5. Check what each change would do to revenue, quality and safety.

The full trees are in the cost reduction framework and the process framework, and where to look for cost savings lists the levers.

Find the constraint before you automate

An online grocery warehouse receives 600 orders a day. Each step has a different daily capacity:

StepCapacity (orders a day)
Picking750
Packing620
Dispatch580

The warehouse can only ship as many orders as its slowest step allows: 580. That leaves 20 orders a day unshipped, and the backlog grows by 100 orders every five-day week. Faster picking equipment would make picking look impressive and change nothing at the end of the line.

Fix dispatch first. If a change lifts it to 680 orders a day, packing at 620 becomes the limit. That is still above the 600 orders arriving, so the backlog stops growing, with 20 orders a day of headroom. If demand is set to rise, packing is the next step to work on. Operations improvement is a loop: fix the binding constraint, measure the whole system, repeat.

The trap most people fall into

Cutting costs that carry revenue. A sales team, a service desk or a quality check can look like overhead and still pay for itself. Suppose cutting part of a sales team saves $2M a year but loses $5M of revenue at a 50% contribution margin. Contribution falls by $2.5M, so the "saving" loses the client $0.5M.

Weak: "Labour is the biggest cost, so I'd cut headcount by 10%."
Strong: "Labour is 40% of costs, but most of it is in dispatch, which is our bottleneck. Cutting there would lose orders. I'd look first at packaging and freight, where we're above peers, and protect anything that drives sales."

Two prompts to try

A telecom company's customer complaints have tripled in six months.

Show the answer
  • What they complain about: billing, network, installation, support; which category grew.
  • Who complains: new or existing customers; region, product, sales channel.
  • What changed: new billing system, price rise, outsourcing; timing against the rise.
  • How we handle them: share resolved on the first call; time to fix, repeat complaints.

Where to start: what changed six months ago. A tripling rarely happens without a trigger.

The trap: hiring more call-centre staff before finding the cause.

A furniture factory's defect rate rose from 2% to 6%.

Show the answer
  • Where defects appear: which product, line, process step and shift.
  • Materials: supplier changes, wood quality; storage and humidity.
  • People: new or temporary staff, training; overtime and fatigue.
  • Machines and process: maintenance, settings, wear; new equipment or faster line speed.

Where to start: where defects appear. Narrowing it to one step usually points to the cause.

Size it: the factory now scraps or reworks three times as many items, 6 in every 100 instead of 2.

The trap: adding more inspection at the end instead of fixing the cause.
